messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane is a 74-year-old editor who came to treatment months after the end of a violent relationship that had left him living in a state of constant alarm. He is a Māori American man who had spent most of his adult life working carefully with other people’s words, and he described the irony that he could still line-edit a manuscript with precision while feeling unable to make sense of what had happened in his own home. During the final year of the relationship, arguments with his partner often turned on correction and criticism. A small comment about how he had loaded the dishwasher, how he had phrased something, or how he had “done it wrong” could escalate without warning. He remembers one assault in particular not as a continuous story but as a series of stark images: his partner’s face tightening as she corrected him, a hand shoving him backward, the edge of a table, the flash of her arm raised again. Those moments still come to him as isolated pictures rather than a full memory, and when they do he is flooded with rage. At times the memory feels so strange and detached that he says it is as if it belongs to someone else, some older man he is watching from outside.

After he left, the world narrowed around the things that could set him off. Being corrected by anyone became dangerous terrain. In the publishing office, if a younger colleague suggested a change to his edits or pointed out a missed citation, Tane would feel his body tense before he had even fully registered the comment. Scenes of violence on television had a similar effect, and on the rare occasions he caught sight of his former partner in the neighborhood, the rest of the day was gone. In those moments he would immediately try to get away from whatever reminded him of her, bury himself in work, turn on the radio, switch tasks, do anything to distract himself. He also worked hard not to feel too much of anything, because strong emotion seemed to open the door to the worst of it. The trigger and the reaction had become almost fused: criticism, violence, or any cue of the offender, and Tane was already reaching to shut down, look away, and mentally move elsewhere.

What frightened him was not only the surge of distress but what came with it. A correction from a coworker could call up one of those visual fragments so abruptly that he would lose the thread of the conversation. Seeing a violent scene in a film could pull back the same few pictures of the assault, vivid and disjointed. When he encountered his former partner unexpectedly, the memory did not unfold as a past event; it arrived as those frozen moments, accompanied by explosive anger and an eerie sense that the experience was not fully his own. He had come to believe that something about him had made the abuse possible, that this had happened because of the sort of person he was. Beneath that was a more corrosive conviction: that he had been reduced to an object in that relationship, handled and corrected rather than regarded as a person. When the memory surfaced in that dissociated, fragmented way, it seemed to confirm those beliefs. The alien quality of it fit too easily with his fear that he had somehow been erased, and each burst of rage on recall felt to him like further proof that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again.

Over the following months, his efforts to manage the aftermath began to trap him inside it. He avoided streets where he might see his former partner and asked a neighbor to pick up groceries if he thought she might be nearby. At work he kept interactions brief and deflected editorial discussions that might involve disagreement. He distracted himself compulsively—crossword puzzles, late-night news, rearranging drafts on his desktop—anything that could keep the images from settling. But the more he cut himself off from reminders and from strong feeling, the less connected the memories became. They stayed as disconnected snapshots, returning without context and with the same violent anger. He noticed that after a day spent frantically keeping busy, a mild criticism could feel even sharper, almost preloaded with danger, and he became quicker to spot offense in ordinary exchanges. His world as an editor, once built around careful revision, had turned into a place full of perceived threat.

These habits also deepened the way he saw himself. Because he could not tolerate reminders or emotion, he began to take this as evidence that he was permanently damaged, no longer fully human in the way he had been before. He told himself that a stronger or better man would have left sooner, would not still be rattled by a corrected sentence or a glimpse across the street. That self-blame made the memories harsher when they came, and the harsher they felt, the more urgently he tried to push them away. Even his attempts to avoid offender cues seemed to make them more powerful; the neighborhood felt smaller, criticism at work more loaded, violence in media more impossible to brush off.

He finally sought help after snapping at a junior editor who had gently corrected a date in a manuscript. Tane had gone rigid, seen again the raised arm and the table edge, and spent the next hour hiding in the restroom in a fury he could barely explain. He was shaken by how quickly he had disappeared into those images and by how little of ordinary feeling seemed available to him outside anger and numbness. What he wants most is to stop living as if every correction means danger is about to break over him. What he fears most is that the abuse has revealed something final about him—that he is, in his own words, “the kind of man this happens to,” and that he will never again feel like a full person in his own life.
